newsitem.title: USA: Great Lakes airline hopes for flights Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Great Lakes airline hopes for flights Thursday.

text.p: Great Lakes Aviation, a Midwest commuter airline that grounded flights after federal inspectors alleged it operated unworthy aircraft, said it hoped to resume some flights by Thursday.

"Assuming everything goes as we expect it to, we hope to have some limited operations in the air on Thursday," Dick Fontaine, senior vice president of marketing for Great Lakes said in an interview Monday.
Great Lakes, based in Spencer, Iowa, voluntarily suspended all flights Friday evening after the Federal Aviation Administration told the carrier it planned to suspend its operating authority.

The airline, which operates commuter flights for United Airlines and Midway Airlines, said it was having aircraft inspections done at its Spencer facility and was concentrating on getting the newer of its 53 twin-engine turboprop aircraft back in the air.
"If we could get three airplanes up in the air (Thursday), then we would have between 20 and 25 flights," Fontaine said.
It operates 500 flights a day, carries about 887,000 passengers annually and serves 82 cities across the United States and three in Mexico, according to the FAA.
The FAA said in a statement issued Saturday that inspections found the airline allowed personnel who were not properly trained and qualified to perform aircraft maintenance.
"The FAA alleges that the airline operated unairworthy aircraft," it said in its statement.

An FAA spokeswoman said Monday the regulatory agency had been working over the weekend on developing a consent decree with Great Lakes, which operates as United Express and Midway Connection. The decree would outline the steps Great Lakes needs to take to resume operation, she said.
Great Lakes said over the weekend it had been in discussions with the FAA about the safety of its aircraft, but did not expect the FAA to suspend its operating authority.

"This process accelerated in the last couple of days," Great Lakes chief executive Douglas Voss told Reuters Saturday. "We did not expect it. We had discussions and due to their (FAA) lack of confidence in status of the aircraft, we elected that we would take the airplanes into maintenance bases and essentially begin a review to be certain there's no question regarding the airworthiness of the aircraft."

The FAA said its action was not related to last November's accident in Quincy, Illinois, when a Great Lakes-operated United Express plane collided with a small aircraft killing 14 people. It was Great Lakes' first crash in more than 20 years of operation.

Last month, the company reported a net loss for 1996 of $12.8 million, due in part to a special charge of $1.5 million to write down the value of its spare parts inventory. In March, Great Lakes said it was experiencing liquidity difficulties and in talks with creditors.
